name: MicroEnergy Credits – Integrated Cooking & Space  Heating Carbon Mitigation Program – Bhutan
description:
The project aims to provide households and institutions in Bhutan with electric cooking and space-heating technologies to reduce GHG emissions from the use of firewood, biomass, and fossil fuels. Developed under GS, the project will deliver verified emission reductions and socio-economic benefits.

For cooking, the project targets low-income households, schools, monasteries, fodder preparation, and small commercial establishments, including rural and high-altitude communities. In the absence of the project, cooking needs are primarily met through firewood, traditional stoves, and LPG, resulting in emissions, pressure on forest resources, and indoor air pollution. The project promotes efficient electric cooking technologies, including induction and infrared cookstoves powered by grid electricity. This transition reduces fuel consumption and emissions while improving indoor air quality, reducing cooking time and costs, and enhancing health and well-being.

For space heating, the programme promotes the replacement of traditional biomass-based heating systems with efficient electric heaters, particularly in colder regions where firewood is the primary heating fuel. The intervention reduces fuel use, emissions, and pressure on forests while improving thermal comfort, indoor air quality, and living conditions. It also reduces the time and costs associated with fuel collection and purchase, especially benefiting women and supporting Bhutan’s low-carbon development objectives.
gsf_standards_version: Gold Standard for the Global Goals

name: VPA 1: Kisan Kalpa: Cultivating Sustainable Income Pathways for Farmers
description:
The primary objective of the Programme of Activities (PoA) is to establish and manage 10,000 ha of agroforestry plantations on croplands across the states of Gujarat and Rajasthan through the implementation of multiple Voluntary Project Activities (VPAs). The PoA aims to promote sustainable land-use practices by introduction of diverse tree species. Through active engagement with local farmers and stakeholders, the PoA initiative will not only sequester approximately 2,433,999 tonnes of CO2 equivalent over the crediting period but also plays a crucial role in developing resilient agroforestry systems that not only restore ecological balance but also deliver long-term social and economic benefits to local farmer communities.
The first real case VPA under this PoA, implemented a small scale agroforestry plantation of 98 ha which sequesters 10,889 tonnes of CO2 equivalent over the crediting period across multiple districts of Gujarat, India, which involves the plantation of multiple agroforestry species on agricultural land. By actively engaging local farmers, the VPA seeks to create resilient agroforestry plantations that generate long term ecological, economic and social benefits for the community.
gsf_standards_version: Gold Standard for the Global Goals

name: GS10789-GS11673-RVPA-121: Efficient and Clean Cooking for households in Nigeria
description: This VPA deploys efficient improved cookstoves (ICS), reducing woody biomass consumption for Urban and peri-urban households in the Republic of Nigeria. The scenario existing prior to the implementation of the project is the use of very inefficient traditional cookstoves or 3- stone fires, consuming a lot of non-renewable charcoal and firewood. The high biomass consumption has negative impacts on the environment leading to deforestation and land degradation, Greenhouse Gas Emissions (GHG) emissions, loss of soil fertility and soils’ reduced ability of water retention. Further, indoor air pollution through health-damaging pollutants while combusting firewood and charcoal result in diseases like e.g. pneumonia, stroke, ischemic heart diseases, chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases and lung cancer.

name: Pakistan Low Carbon Rice Programme
description:
Net Zero Ag Limited plans a Programme of Activities that aims to reduce methane emissions associated with conventional farming (CF) techniques. The first small-scale project activities will start in Narowal and Mandi Bahauddin, Pakistan on May 2026.  
Rice cultivation is one of the main GHG sources within the agriculture sector and generates approximately 8.5 MtCO2e of methane per year — roughly 2% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Conventional flooding-based production practices generate significant methane emissions and consume large volumes of fresh water. The programme will introduce the technique of alternate wetting and drying (AWD) to rice farmers in Pakistan. By adaptation of the technique, controlled irrigation strategy implemented will significantly reduce methane emissions, water use, and pumping costs.

name: India Roots Collective: Community-Led Agroforestry & Landscape Restoration
description:
The project supports smallholder farmers in integrating agroforestry practices into existing agricultural lands to improve livelihoods, strengthen ecosystem resilience, and promote sustainable land management.
The project involves planting and maintaining a mix of native fruit and timber tree species within farming systems. Fruit trees provide regular income and food security benefits, while timber species offer long-term economic value. These interventions also improve soil health, reduce soil erosion, enhance soil moisture retention, and increase vegetation cover.
The project contributes to climate change mitigation through carbon sequestration in tree biomass and enhancement of soil organic carbon, generating measurable and verifiable greenhouse gas removals under the Gold Standard Land Use and Forests (LUF) framework. By diversifying farm income and restoring degraded landscapes, the project aims to deliver long-term climate, environmental, and socio-economic benefits for participating rural communities.

name: VPA1: Incentivizing Rice Farming Communities to Transition to Low-Emissions Agriculture in India
description:
The project enables rice growing farmers in Andhra Pradesh to transition from conventional continuously flooded rice cultivation to Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD). The core purpose is to reduce methane emissions from paddy fields while improving water efficiency, strengthening climate resilience, and increasing farmer livelihoods through a single scalable intervention. In the first instance the project is implemented in the Srikakulam and  vizinagaram Andhra Pradesh in 5,041  ha of land which reduces 6,710  tCO2e/year.

Detail climate change mitigation/adaptation contributions
Mitigation: The project delivers climate mitigation benefits by reducing methane generation in paddy fields. AWD shortens the duration of continuous flooding, allowing aerobic soil conditions to form, which:
Significantly reduces methane emissions, the dominant emission source in irrigated paddy
Lowers energy-related emissions due to reduced irrigation pumping demand
Prevents soil carbon loss caused by over-flooding and anaerobic conditions

The transition is expected to generate substantial emission reductions across all participating fields under the project boundary.

Adaptation: AWD strengthens climate resilience in farming systems and communities by:
Reducing water consumption, helping farmers cope with erratic rainfall and declining groundwater
Improving soil aeration and root development, enabling crops to better tolerate climatic

description:
The project enables rice growing farmers in Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Telangana, Tamilnadu, West Bengal, Odisha and Chhattisgarh to transition from conventional continuously flooded rice cultivation to Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD). The core purpose is to reduce methane emissions from paddy fields while improving water efficiency, strengthening climate resilience, and increasing farmer livelihoods through a single scalable intervention. In the first instance the project is implemented in the Srikakulam and vizinagaram villages of Andhra Pradesh in 5,041 ha of land which reduces 6,710  tCO2e/year.

Detail climate change mitigation/adaptation contributions
Mitigation: The project delivers climate mitigation benefits by reducing methane generation in paddy fields. AWD shortens the duration of continuous flooding, allowing aerobic soil conditions to form, which:
Significantly reduces methane emissions, the dominant emission source in irrigated paddy
Lowers energy-related emissions due to reduced irrigation pumping demand
Prevents soil carbon loss caused by over-flooding and anaerobic conditions

The transition is expected to generate substantial emission reductions across all participating fields under the project boundary.

Adaptation: AWD strengthens climate resilience in farming systems and communities by:
Reducing water consumption, helping farmers cope with erratic rainfall and declining groundwater
Improving soil aeration and root development, enabling crops to better tolerate climatic stress
Lowering irrigation costs and farm expenses, increasing financial resilience
Improving access to technical support and knowledge through farmer training and field demonstrations
By promoting a climate-responsive irrigation practice, the project supports long-term adaptation to rising temperatures and water scarcity in Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Telangana, Tamilnadu, West Bengal, Odisha and Chhattisgarh of Indian states.

name: GHG Emissions Reduction & Sequestration - Afforestation/Reforestation - Future Radici (Emilia Romagna 2)
description: The Real Case VPA Future Radici, Emilia Romagna 2 represents a pivotal and strategic initiative within the broader framework of the Programme of Activities (PoA) Future Radici. The project spans a total area of 104.12 hectares across two agricultural estates: Raveda, and Portonovo. These lands are owned by Leone Alato SpA. The project envisions the planting of approximately 124,500 trees, with the goal of transforming these agricultural lands into thriving, biodiverse forest ecosystems. The primary objective is to establish native and ecologically rich forest environments through a combination of afforestation and agroforestry practices. These practices are carefully tailored to the pedoclimatic and ecological characteristics of each site, ensuring that the interventions enhance biodiversity, support complex habitats, and maximize long-term carbon sequestration. The forest models adopted in this project are non-extractive, the harvesting of timber or biomass is explicitly excluded. This commitment extends for a minimum duration of 60 years. To quantify the carbon absorption, the project will rely on methodologies recommended by the IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change). These methods will be calibrated using national and regional data. The goal is to produce credits that are measurable, verifiable, and directly linked to positive outcomes in both biodiversity and social impact.

name: GS13053-Transforming Coffee Production Systems in Brazil with Agroforestry to Store Carbon, Regenerate Ecosystems, and Improve Farmer Livelihoods in Mantiqueira de Minas
description:
In partnership with Hanns R. Neumann Stiftung, GrowGrounds is transforming coffee monocultures in Brazil’s Mantiqueira region into regenerative agroforestry systems that sequester carbon, restore biodiversity, and strengthen farm resilience. Over a 30-year period, the initiative will convert 500 to 1,500 hectares of coffee land and engage more than 200 smallholder farmers. By integrating trees into coffee systems compatible with mechanized harvesting and cattle grazing, the project provides a scalable model that improves soil health, enhances climate resilience, and supports landscape restoration.

Beyond carbon sequestration, the project generates strong social and environmental benefits. Farmers receive 70% of carbon revenues, benefit from improved working conditions through shade-grown systems, and gain diversified long-term income opportunities.

The project area borders the Serra do Papagaio State Park, a protected area of approx. 22,917 hectares within the Mantiqueira Mountain Range, a critical water source for southeastern Brazil. The park conserves remnants of the Atlantic Forest biome, one of the world’s most biodiverse and threatened ecosystems. To assess biodiversity impacts and guide monitoring, the project applies the IUCN's RHINO framework, with a focus on key species including the Maldonado Redbelly Toad, Buffy-tufted-ear marmoset, Ochre-breasted Pipit, Vinaceous-breasted Amazon, Sickle-winged Nightjar, and Luderwaldt's Highland Frog.

name: AWD Methane Reduction Project in Cambodia
description:
The Amru Rice AWD Project in Cambodia supports the adoption of Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) in irrigated rice cultivation to reduce methane emissions while maintaining stable yields and farmer livelihoods. The project replaces continuous flooding with controlled wetting and drying cycles, using water-level pipes to guide irrigation timing and ensure safe drainage thresholds. By reducing anaerobic soil conditions in paddy fields, AWD can significantly lower methane emissions while also improving irrigation water efficiency.
The project is expected to scale to beyond 20,000 hectares. The project is being co-developed by Amru Rice Cambodia and CarbonFarm, with both parties acting as project proponents. Amru Rice Cambodia leads on-ground implementation, while CarbonFarm supports as a technical partner through digital MRV tools, including satellite imagery, AI-based field monitoring, and selected IoT devices to strengthen data traceability.

name: GS23679-VPA1 Amazi Water Carbon Credit Program in Burundi
description: Amazi Water Carbon Credit Program in Burundi acts as a bridge between climate action and community development. This program allows communities to gain access to safe water through boreholes and solar-powered supply systems, leaving out the need to boil water using firewood or charcoal. This translates into measurable emission savings, which can be certified as carbon credits under the Gold Standard. Through this program, communities of Burundi enjoy uninterrupted access to safe water, which reduces waterborne diseases, improves public health, and protect forests by reducing demand for firewood, while cutting carbon emissions that contribute to climate change. The program provides a mechanism to sustain water infrastructure, improve health outcomes, protect the environment, and empower communities, all while contributing to global efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
gsf_standards_version: Gold Standard for the Global Goals

name: Belize Coastal Sargassum Resilience and Circularity Project
description: The Belize Coastal Sargassum Resilience and Circularity Project aims to intercept and process sargassum biomass and eligible biodegradable organic matter to avoid methane emissions from uncontrolled decomposition and landfill disposal. The project combines controlled aerobic treatment, decentralized organic waste processing, and circular resource recovery to transform intercepted biomass into beneficial products, including biochar-enriched compost for local use. Implemented initially in Caye Caulker, Belize, in collaboration with local stakeholders, the project is designed to strengthen coastal resilience, support sustainable land management, reduce environmental impacts associated with sargassum accumulation, and contribute to measurable climate mitigation outcomes under Gold Standard methodologies.

name: GS23156-GS13112 RVPA-1 VPA-15 Improved Rice Cultivation in Bangladesh
description: The purpose of this project is to modernize paddy cultivation in Bangladesh by promoting and implementing the alternate wetting and drying (AWD) method in project farms/areas. The AWD method promoted under the project is designed to optimize water usage in paddy cultivation by alternating periods of wetting and drying. This technique reduces water consumption and improves soil aeration, as a result methane emissions from paddy fields are significantly reduced contributing to lower greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions.
